newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing merger flouts anti-trust law -Cresson.
newsitem.headline: Boeing merger flouts anti-trust law -Cresson.

text.p: French European Commission member Edith Cresson said on Thursday Boeing Co's merger with McDonnell Douglas was out of line with competition law and would give the merged group a near or total monopoly in some markets.
The European Commission in Brussels approved the merger in principle this week in return for certain concessions.
Cresson, one of two French members of the Commission, was quoted by afternoon paper Le Monde as saying in an interview that the concessions were not negligible.

But, she said, "Beyond the position it will have in large capacity planes, Boeing is acquiring a monopoly in 100-seater craft and a virtual monopoly, 90 percent of the world market, in freight transport planes."

"Whatever you say, this amounts to an infringement of competition law, far more serious than that which would have happened with the acquisition which was prohibited at the time of De Havilland by ATR," she was quoted as saying.

The European Commission obtained wide merger control powers in 1990 and used them for the first time in 1991 to prohibit the acquisition of Canadian aircraft maker De Havilland by ATR, a consortium of France's Aerospatiale and Italy's Alenia.
Asked what the reaction in Europe should be, Cresson said Boeing rival Airbus, the European aircraft consortium, should "markedly" reinforce cooperation between its member companies.

"With its monopoly position in some market segments and its extreme superiority in others as well as the benefits of money on the military side, Beoing is going to be able to cut prices. Strengthening Airbus is absolutely vital," she said.
The European Commission, which votes by majority among its member commissioners from the 15 EU countries, is due to issue its formal decision on the Boeing tie-up next week.
French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Friday France needed more details on the $15 billion tie-up when asked if he thought enough concessions had been extracted from the U.S. giant.
"Boeing's aeronautical position was already dominant. This merger...naturally poses problems," he said on French radio.
